speechtext:
Mr. JEAN FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 30, to repeal the Employment and Social Insurance Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am moving the introduction and the first reading of this bill to repeal the Employment and Social Insurance Act.. Last June this legislation was K.O'd by the Supreme Court of Canada and on January 28 the privy council gave it its coup de grace. Since February 1 this legislative corpse has been lying in state on the order paper. It is too late to revive it or even to embalm it. This bill is intended to be a grave digger as it is high time that this legislation was buried.
If I may be permitted, I should like to give a little experience I had just recently. Three commissioners were appointed under this act, and I was told the other day by the government that the judgment of the privy council

decided the status of these gentlemen. I drew your honour's attention to the fact that one of these commissioners had been canvassing from door to door among the members and I inquired if he had a licence as a parliamentary agent. I went up to my room and I saw him in the corridor speaking to a stenographer. He was probably trying to canvass her. He told me that he wanted to see one of my colleagues, whose office was beside mine. I happened to know from that hon. gentleman that this former commissioner, who had received a salary of $9,000 per year for doing nothing, was looking for another soft job paying at least $5,500. I called down to the main door to have a constable sent up. When the constable came up I asked him to ask this gentleman if he had a licence as a parliamentary agent. The gentleman gave no answer to the constable. I then went over myself and I said, "What are you doing here, bothering the members, running from room to room?" He saidi, "I want to see such and such a member." I said, "I know that is false because that member told me he wanted nothing to do with you, that you were just looking for a soft job." I said, "Have you a card as a parliamentary agent?" And he said, "No." I then asked the constable to escort him out of this parliamentary building, which he did. I had to do this thing myself, but I did it, and this gentleman is now out of the building. Therefore I want the commission put out of the picture also. I move the introduction of this bill, seconded by the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. St. Pere), the respected whip of Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course my hon. friend can insist upon introducing this bill and the others that follow it on the order paper, but I should like to say that the legislation which these bills are intended to repeal has no operative effect whatever and no purpose would be served by taking it out of our statutes. On the other hand, some of this legislation might be amended and by cooperation with the provinces be brought within the sphere of federal jurisdiction. As to the others there is the possibility of amending the British North America Act, still in cooperation with the provinces, to make the legislation effective.
As there is no purpose whatever to be served by repealing this act, which is a dead letter as it is, and as it may be useful in some way to keep it there, perhaps my hon. friend would agree to let the statute remain as it is now and allow the government to deal with it in the best interests of the house and of the people.

Business of the House

Answering what my hon. leader from Quebec has said, I do not intend to kill that legislation, because it is dead now; I am only trying to bury it-that is the difference. If we have a dead letter on the statute book it is just as well to dispense with it, because otherwise when there is a revision of the dominion statutes these acts will be included.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, never.

I think it is just as well to allow this bill, which is only seeking to repeal another act, receive its first reading. Never did a government object to the first reading of a bill except when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was Prime Minister. I hope my hon. friend the Minister of Justice has no objection to the first reading being given.
Mr. LAPOINTE (Quebec East); I have no objection. The hon. member has a right to introduce it, but it is useless.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
There is an extraordinary news item in the Montreal Gazette of to-day, to the effect that unemployed who desire assistance in settling on the land will be refused aid if they have "advanced ideas" or have been members of a communist or socialist organization ; that aldermen at the city hall were so informed yesterday by the Auger-Rogers foack-to-the-land plan forwarded them by the provincial ministry of colonization. The regulation reads in part:
The would-be colonist of "advanced ideas" who has previously taken part in a communist or socialist organization cannot be accepted.
In view of the fact that the opposition in the British House of Commons is a socialist opposition, and that New Zealand, a sister dominion, is under a socialist government, it seems to me an extraordinary thing that any regulation of this kind can be put forward in one of our provinces. I am aware that later in the article the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) is reported as saying he knows nothing

Labour Dispute
of the matter, but I do not think that that statement of his, as given to the press, is quite enough, and I ask whether the minister will give the house the assurance that the government will give no assistance to any scheme that discriminates against any individual because of his political affiliations or his religious beliefs.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): All agreements with the provinces concerning unemployment relief contain a provision that there shall be no discrimination with respect to race, religion or political affiliation. In my opinion no regulations under any agreement can be made which are contrary to that provision. I hope that will satisfy my hon. friend.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT DOCK FACILITIES AT VANCOUVER AND UNLOADING OF MOTORSHIP BELLINGHAM

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: GOVERNMENT DOCK FACILITIES AT VANCOUVER AND UNLOADING OF MOTORSHIP BELLINGHAM
speechtext: I desire to direct a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) with reference to a situation in the port of Vancouver. I have received to-day a telegram, a copy of which has been sent, I believe, to the minister. It states that the motorship Bellingham, American registry, arrived in the port of Vancouver yesterday with a cargo of fish consigned to the Canadian Fishing Company Limited. The owners of the vessel wished to have the International Longshoremen's Association of Vancouver discharge the cargo. The Canadian Fishing Company will not allow that to be done at their dock. The owners of the vessel are willing to have the cargo discharged at any other dock. Mr. Burns, who I believe is the port manager at the government docks, advised the International Longshoremen's Association that he is not in a position to say that the facilities of the government docks will be available if members of the International Longshoremen's Association are employed to unload the ship. Could the minister give the house any information with regard to this matter, and state whether the shipping federation completely control the men who are to discharge and load ships in the port of Vancouver, and particularly on government docks?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT DOCK FACILITIES AT VANCOUVER AND UNLOADING OF MOTORSHIP BELLINGHAM
speechtext:
I received notice of the hon. member's question and telephoned our port manager to-day. The facts are not exactly as stated by the hon. member. It is true that the steamship Bellingham arrived at Vancouver yesterday with a cargo of 250,000 pound? frozen fish
consigned to the Canadian Fishing Company Limited, but the contract for the carrying of this cargo calls for the running of the cargo at the dock of the Canadian Fishing Company Limited, Vancouver. After unloading about twenty-five per cent of the cargo the ship's crew discontinued servicing the winches,' thereby causing a stoppage of work on the part of the longshoremen. The reason given for this action by the ship's crew is that the longshoremen working the ship are not members of the International Longshoremen's Association. On the other hand, the Canadian Fishing Company Limited refuses to permit I.L.A. men to discharge cargo at its dock. It is to be noted that the Canadian Fishing Company Limited is not a member of the local shipping federation. Representatives of the local International Longshoremen's Association called upon Mr. Burns stating that the reason for the action of the ship's crew was that before leaving Ketchikan for Vancouver the crew had been assured that the cargo would be unloaded by I.L.A. men. They then wished to ascertain whether Burns would permit the unloading of this cargo at the harbour board's fish dock. Mr. Burns pointed out that this was quite impossible for the reason that the water depth of the fish dock would be insufficient, it being about ten feet only, to accommodate the steamship Bellingham. Moreover, the landing of the cargo elsewhere than on the Canadian Fishing Company's dock would create a breach of the contract between the vessel owner and the company under which the latter could refuse delivery of the cargo; in other words, before any arrangement could be made to unload the cargo at any dock, arrangements would have to be made for the disposal of the cargo. It is perishable cargo, and if it is unloaded at our docks and thrown out ihere it would belong to no one. We should like to know before it is unloaded what the disposition of it is to be, and who is to pay the charges.

The government has decided that two new ships shall be purchased for the protection of both our coasts. I take it for granted that the government's views in this respect are sound, but on the other hand we must not forget that the coasts on both sides are hundreds of miles long and there are many bays on the Pacific as well as on the Atlantic seaboard, besides the gulf of St. Lawrence and the St. Lawrence river. It is necessary, therefore, for the new ships to be the most effective and speedy. Our entire fleet on each side will consist of one man of war only, and the life of that man of war is that of a dog, twelve years. I submit, therefore, that when the government decides to purchase one battleship for the defence of each coast the ships should be the most efficient and the speediest, and ships that can give the best service. I believe hon. members will agree with me in that. I do not object to the vote because it is too large-and I am wondering whether there will be an amendment to reduce it- but I do object to it because it is too small. We do not need second hand ships, and if the government is of the opinion that we must have ships to defend our shores they should be the very best. If we have a small ship let it be the latest one from the shipyards. I cannot therefore vote for any amendment to reduce this item, because I do not think it is large enough; and for that reason I cannot support this item in the estimates.

Will the minister explain
this vote and tell us what proportion will go to the Pacific?

Perhaps

What will be the total expenditure for naval protection? The estimates are divided into three parts; we have roughly $19,000,000 for land forces, and about

$11,000,000 for air forces, and I understand there is about $5,000,000 for naval protection. What will be the total for naval protection-$5,000,000 or $7,000,000?

The two destroyers were really under this fiscal year's expenditures because negotiations to purchase them were completed last year and they will be charged against expenditures for 1936-37. The total of $2,000,000 should be added to the figure shown for the present year.

I did not make myself clear. What I want to find out is what increase in the estimates will be necessary as a result of the expenditures we are incurring this year for increased naval armaments and new ships. Will that mean an increased future outlay each year?

Supply-Defence-Naval Services

It will
be the difference in the number of ratings and stores necessary for the new destroyers as against the old ones. The new ships are considerably larger and will require an increased personnel. There will be an increase personnel for the new mine sweepers and training schooner. Otherwise there is no increase.
What will be the increase?
About $300,000 or $400,000, but that is subject to correction.

Mr. Chairman, I did not take part in the debate which took place last week on the amendment presented by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), but the public and this house knew very well where I stood on this question of armament. However, I wish to avail myself of the present discussion of the military estimates to say once more that I am against any direct or indirect contribution to extraterritorial wars. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lake St. John-Roberval (Mr. Sylvestre):
That item 67 of the national defence estimates be reduced by $1,832,310.

Mr. Chairman, I have no objection to my hon. friend moving his amendment, but the reason he sets forth is not fair. He states that he is against extraterritorial wars, but these estimates which we are discussing have no connection whatever with extra-territorial wars.

I want to tell the committee that I am entirely satisfied with the explanations given to me by the minister a moment ago. The committee will see in due course what to do with the supplementary estimates in regard to second hand ships.
What is the cost of the mine sweepers?

The
amount included in the estimates this year is three quarters of a million dollars. The estimated cost is one quarter of a million each, a total of one million, but it is not anticipated that they can be finished during the present year.
How many mine sweepers will be constructed on the Pacific coast?
That has not been finally decided, but at least one, possibly two.
Can the minister say when he expects the two new ships to be delivered to this country?

They
were commissioned as Canadian vessels a week ago and are expected to sail from England about March 12.
What is the increase in the tonnage?

The details of the new destroyers are as follows:
Displacement, 1,375 tons as against 1,075 for the old Champlain and Vancouver which have been demilitarized. The dimensions of the ships are as follows:
Length, 317} feet as against 275} feet.

What is the usual period of usefulness of a ship of that kind, and when were these ships completed?
The estimated life of a destroyer of this type is about twenty years. They were built in April, 1932, they are a little over four years old.

We are told that this is a part of the defence plan for Canada, which is supposed to be an adequate plan. What function are these destroyers, these new ships, designed to perform? What work are they particularly required to do under the plan set forth by the minister?

That I think is more or less obvious. It will be patrol and defence of our territorial waters, harbour mouths and shipping terminals on both coasts. I do not for the moment pretend that this is an ample naval force for that purpose, but it is at least a force which would cooperate with other forces in giving some reasonable protection.
There will be only these two destroyers doing that patrol work?

We shall have four modern destroyers when the other two are here.

Supply-Defence-Naval Services
But there are only two on each coast?
That has been the case so far.
Does the minister really consider that two patrol boats on each coast can defend this country or maintain our neutrality?
I think they can do quite a lot in cooperation with the other services. It is much better than nothing at all.
Would the minister not think as a matter of policy that if the same amount were spent say for air defences it would give better results?

No, in
the cooperative work of the various services it is necessary to have surface ships as well as air services, and these as my hon. friend will agree are on a very modest scale indeed.

In answering the hon.
member for Winnipeg North a moment ago as to the increased annual cost on account of equipment the minister said that there would be a certain increase in cost arising out of the increased ratings. I am not very familiar with these terms. What does "increased ratings" mean? Does it mean the additional number of men?
Yes.
Would there not also be an increase in cost arising out of the larger ships and more efficient equipment?
Yes, possibly, that is so.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to reiterate my opposition to any increase in the national defence estimates, and I believe, moreover, that the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Dubois) has stated the reasons why just as well as I could do it myself. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), when he stated that he may, each year, ask for increases, depending on conditions then prevailing. The minister said that
the maintenance of the two new ships will perhaps amount to $300,000 each. Is that included in the present estimate?

Royal Canadian Air Force

Expenses in connection with the general maintenance and training of the permanent and non-permanent active air force, and provision of facilities therefor, $11,391,650.
Does this vote include expenditures for landing fields? Have landing fields through to the coast been completed?

Landing fields would not ordinarily come under the Department of National Defence but, as the hon. member will realize, under the civil aviation branch of the Department of Transport. I presume the hon. member has reference to the matter we discussed last year.
Yes.

That was well under way some time ago. I do not know whether the Minister of Transport can answer it, but there was definite progress made with reference to it before the transfer from the Department of National Defence to the Department of Transport took place.

I just wish to remind the minister that a discussion took place last year with respect to a landing field at Chilliwack, and at that time he promised it would be proceeded with. The latest information I have is that nothing has been done, not even to the extent of securing the land.
I think definite steps were taken before the transfer was effected, but I shall look into the matter, with my colleague, and inform the hon. member.
Would the minister tell the committee the number of machines the government has in service in the air defence of Canada?

At the present time the total in Canada is 182 aeroplanes. There are 8 fighter Siskins now obsolete; 18 army cooperation of which 15 Atlas, now practically obsolete, and 3 Avro No. 626 ; 4 Vancouver flying boats, which are obsolescent; 7 new torpedo bombing Blackburn "Sharks," only 4 of which have been delivered so far, but which are modern service planes; 105 various types of training planes, many obsolete, and 40 transportation planes of different types used on various government services, particularly civil government air operations, making a total of 182.

Supply-Defence-Air Force
The present estimate provides for an increase of 102 planes, as follows: 12 fighter planes, 3 army cooperation planes, 7 flying boats, 24 bomber planes, of which 18 are used Wapiti planes, and 6 new Avro No. 626, 11 torpedo bombing planes, 18 coastal reconnaissance planes, and 27 training planes.
How many aeroplanes has the minister purchased since assuming office?

Since
April 1, 1934, the following were ordered: October 3, 1934, 10 Atlas airframes from the air ministry; on May 27, 1935, 10 Civet Fleet airframes; on November 18, 1935, 6 Wapiti airframes, from the air ministry; on November 28, 1936, 5 Stranraer aeroplanes, from Canadian Vickers; on September 22, 1936, 10 Fleet trainer airframes; on May 11, 1936,
1 Avro tudor aeroplane, from Armstrong Siddeley; on May 4, 1936, 7 Torpedo "Shark" aeroplanes, from the air ministry; on August 29, 1935, 3 Avro type "626" aeroplanes, from Armstrong Siddeley; on August 23, 1935, 3 Northrop Delta aeroplanes, from Canadian Vickers, for civil government air operations; on August 9, 1935. 2 super-71 Fairchild aeroplanes, from the Canadian Wright Company, and on January 11, 1937, 4 Northrop Delta aeroplanes for civil government operations.
How many of these machines are now being operated by the government?
All the planes as required and suitable, namely 182 of them; but few are modern service planes.
Are any under repair?
Inevitably there are always some under repair.
Some are so obsolete that they could not very well be used by the government for flying purposes?
Not that I know of. Unless they are being repaired for purposes of training, I am not aware of any. Some are obsolete of course.
How does the speed of these planes compare with those of similar types in other countries?

The new planes we are receiving compete favourably with the best in the world, and the new ones being ordered will be modern in every detail -speed, strength and range; in every way they will be the most modem available. In almost every case the types have been advised by the British air ministry.

The Blackburn machines are well known, but I understand that some of the machines purchased here in Ottawa are old and obsolete. Persons conversant with flying claim it would be hazardous for them to be utilized for flying purposes. The question of uniforms should receive the careful attention of the minister and his department, not only with reference to the flying clubs but in connection with the nonpermanent active militia. The day of the khaki uniform has passed. It is a drab, unattractive thing and does not inspire any enthusiasm in the youth of our country. I believe there would be a greater urge to join the various units if our young men knew that they would be outfitted in colourful uniforms. If I might be permitted to refer again to that great city which I represent, Brantford, I would remind the minister that while we have one quite modern armoury, the other building, known as Dalhousie Street armoury, could hardly be described as such. It is simply a commercial building consisting of a basement and three floors. There is supposed to be a shooting range in the cellar, but as that space is mostly taken up with the furnace and piles of storage, it is entirely inadequate for the purpose. The other floors are broken up into small sections, and in order to get from the ground floor to the second or third floors you must go outside and ascend by another stairway. As I said before, the so-called armouries is not in any way worthy of the name. In that armouries there have been located three units, an artillery unit, a machine gun unit, and a cavalry unit. One of them, the artillery unit, the 54th Battery, won the governor general's cup this year, which is the prize given for the very best shooting by any artillery unit in Canada, and I say that a unit that can win such honours is worthy of some consideration as to where they shall be quartered in their home town.
Speaking generally of armouries, I think more consideration should be given to the men in the units. What have we in our armouries to-day? We have a large drill hall containing the officers' quarters, which are usually fairly palatial, and I quite approve of that. I was pleased indeed to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) refer in such splendid terms the other day to the brass hate. We have to have generals; we have to have officers. An army cannot function without generals and officers any more than a factory can function without managers and foremen. Then besides the officers' quarters and the drill hall there is what is known as the sergeants' mess, reasonably good quarters, but only reasonably so. We must pay due regard to the sergeants, the non-commissioned officers throughout the country because they are in many respects the backbone of every militia unit.
But what about the men? Often we find that the men are almost entirely forgotten. At the close of the parade the regiment is dismissed. The officers go to their quarters, the sergeants go to their quarters, and the men-well, only an army expression would describe what they do. They merely break
off and go on their way. I think that more consideration should be given to the men.
I have referred to the uniforms. The officers and the sergeants have dress uniforms but the men have nothing but khaki. They should have something bright and brilliant. When the parade is over, instead of being dismissed and sent on their way, they should have some quarters of their own to which they could go and mingle with their pals.
In conclusion, and to sum up, I would again draw the minister's attention to the fact that in Brantford we have enough men to form a squadron of the air force. I hope that a survey will soon be made of the quarters provided for the various units in Brantford, and generally I would most strongly urge that more colourful uniforms be given to all ranks. And in all cases where a new armoury is being built more consideration should be given to the accommodation which will be known as the men's quarters.

One of the best plans of national defence I believe to be defence from the air. I have been reading a good deal along this line recently, and expert opinion seems to be that there is no effective defence possible from land or sea, that both land and sea forces are vulnerable, but that the air forces are invulnerable except to attack from the air.
I am glad to notice that there are to be twenty-four bombing planes, but there should be several times -that number. It may he of interest to some hon. members to know that in the bombing raids upon London during the great war not one single bombing plane was ever brought down by antiaircraft guns. On the other hand we -are told that bombing planes can hit their mark both on land and sea with very close precision. I think in most countries nowadays the big planes used for civil -aviation are convertible, and some planes built for civil government air operations are convertible for purposes of national defence.

Before the vote is taken I wish to ask a question or two of the minister. Before I do so, however, I Should like to commend him on the very efficient manner in which he placed before the house a few days ago the defence situation, together with an outline of his proposals for improving it. The minister has also defended his estimates in an admirable manner under heavy fire, not only from one section of the opposition; I notice that quite a few " shorts " fell in his direction. The Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence have made it very plain to everyone that the proposed increased armament is for defence purposes only. To me that seems largely self-evident. The scope of our defensive armaments as limited by the estimates precludes the possibility of their being used for offensive action overseas. In other words no serious percentage of the arms and equipment to be provided by this program could be moved outside of the country without weakening our defensive position at home to an extent almost inviting disaster.
Now, sir, our defence program, small though it be, should be viewed in the light of modern conditions. Methods of warfare have changed. They have very largely moved from the land and the water into the air. This condition invites from me at this time what may be considered in some quarters as a preposterous statement; however I give it for what it is worth. There is the possibility that at last the tide has commenced to turn, that modern world armament has reached or will shortly have reached, before the completion of the British defence program, the point where it defeats its own ends. My opinion is based upon certain facts. I repeat that offensive warfare has largely moved from the land and the water into the air. I refer to bombing, whether with gas, explosives, or incendiary and chemical materials. It is largely agreed among competent authorities that especially under weather conditions favourable to the attack no adequate direct defence against bombing has yet been found. But there is the important exception of indirect measures, in other words the fear of certain and effective retaliation. The German general staff-and I refer to it simply to illustrate my point -is quite well aware of what retaliation would mean. They realize that bombing attacks on London or the Midlands or important ports would probably be highly successful in themselves, but at the same time they are just as completely aware that even before their bombers in their hundreds-and there would be hundreds-reach England, as large or a larger number of British bombers

would 'be winging their way to Germany, probably actually passing the enemy squadrons, and would cause unparalleled damage to the cities, towns, ports and important centres in that country.
No one man is responsible for the tragic and utterly crazy military situation that exists to-day. It has grown to its present alarming proportions through factors largely arising out of the treaty of Versailles, and also, as has been mentioned here time and again, through the failure of the League of Nations to function as we all hoped it would. I submit that preparedness is reaching that ultimate point where there is a real possibility that it will defeat its own ends. As one surveys the political and military evidence as it now exists I think the conclusion can be fairly reached that preliminary overtures for some measure of disarmament may be under way before the completion of the British program.
At this point I would direct attention to certain remarks of the Prime Minister in his eloquent speech on Friday last. They were of importance, and cannot receive too much emphasis. At page 1048 of Hansard for last Friday the Prime Minister is reported to have said:
We know whatever the ambitions of their rulers may be that throughout the world the peoples as a whole are anxious to preserve peace. On the whole there has been some improvement, a less tense strain in the international situation, a balancing of forces, a growing recognition on the part of every government of the uncertainties of success and the penalties of failure, a growing readiness too to seek to remove the causes of conflict, the sources of friction, and to realize that in the end war settles nothing even for the victor.
Of course there is the other school of thought which holds the view that world conflict is inevitable. We may rest assured it will not be provoked or commenced by the British commonwealth of nations. Its position is now well known, and can be appropriately described in a sentence from Lincoln's first inaugural speech. I believe this sentence is as fitting as it could be:
This government will not assail you; you can have no conflict, without yourselves being the aggressors.
For the time being the English-speaking people must continue to do their part. This is a matter of first-class importance. As I see it, the British commonwealth of nations is like a chain girdling the earth, but at the same time it is no stronger than its weakest link.
In conclusion may I say that as I view it our minister is simply endeavouring to bring our defences to such a point of efficiency that,

He has shown great courage in laying all his cards on the table and asking for enough money to furnish a modest defence force with that quality and class of arms and equipment to which our Canadian soldiers, sailors, and airmen are justly entitled.
Is it the intention of the department to have considerable eoordinative training between our air squadrons and our naval units?
Yes, that is the intention.

I believe two destroyers will be reporting in April. Is it the intention of the government to have the two new destroyers manoeuvre together, or to have one join the obsolete destroyer on one coast, and the other join the other destroyer?

The
practice in the past has been to have the four destroyers meet annually in West Indies waters for naval training exercises. I presume that will be continued in the future.

The trend of the discussion confirms the suspicions I expressed the other day. We are not discussing preparations for defence ; rather we are discussing preparations for participation in a war of offence. This afternoon we have heard that we should have more colourful uniforms with which to arouse militaristic sentiment in our youth, and that we should have larger armouries instead of emphasis on coastal defence. We have heard the minister describe how the major portion of the expenditures will go for the purchase of mobile equipment, and no emphasis is placed on the necessary part it will play in actual coastal defence. Now we are calmly discussing-and it is being advocated- increased purchases of bombing planes, and it is suggested that bombing planes are necessary for defence. I am anxious to have someone explain to me how, under conditions of modem warfare, a bombing plane could be considered as a defensive weapon. Bombing planes are used to bomb, and surely it is not intended to drop bombs on our own territory. Evidently it is expected we shall engage in measures of retaliation, and drop bombs on innocent women and children in other parts of the world.
What about submarines?

The correct defensive
weapon against 'the submarine is the depth charge. It is inconceivable to me that in Canada we should plan an expedition to retaliate against other countries, and that we should make preparation on such a grand scale 'as to send flight squadrons across the Atlantic or the Pacific to drop bombs on the towns of other countries.
Suppose a foreign country established a base in Canada, what would happen?

That is a remote possibility, and for defence against it bombing planes are not required. To repel the attack of air raiders you must have fighting planes, and fighting planes .are not usually armed with bombs. The point I make is that the discussion indicates that the trend is not towards preparation for defence, but rather for offence, and that all-
No, no.

-All the items presented by the minister indicate careful preparation under advice of experts of the British war office, so that we may take our place in the fine of empire defence. My views in that regard are confirmed by the remarks of the hon. member who has just taken his seat. In .that regard the assurances given by the government stand for naught; for all preparations indicate that steps are being taken in a contrary direction. For these reasons I support -the amendment, and have no scruples in .protesting against the increased expenditure for aviation, advanced largely at the expense of civil aviation, where our young men actually get their technical training. Clearly the expenditure is intended for purposes of offence rather than defence.

So far I have not taken any part in the discussion of these estimates, but I do believe the observations of the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. MacNeil) cannot escape the consideration of the committee. The Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Justice have indicated in no uncertain terms that the program of the government, in these particulars, was actuated by no consideration other than one of national defence. In fairness to my convictions, which I believe are well known in some quarters, I could not possibly vote for any measure which would be for purposes of offensive action.
Why bombing planes, then?

The hon. member has made a very serious charge, one which is not only in contradiction to the undertaking given by



Supply-Defence-Air Force
responsible ministers but clearly involves an issue far out of proportion to anything already mentioned by the hon. member. As one member to another I would ask him if he can substantiate his charge that the estimates are for purposes of offensive action and not fo.r purposes of defence, and not in vague but in specific language, I would ask him to give some justification for his observations.

I will inform the hon. member that the information tabled by the minister during the discussion of the estimates indicates that the major portion of the expenditures is for weapons which may be considered weapons of offence rather than weapons of defence. Greater emphasis is placed upon mobile equipment, which may readily be used for purposes of overseas contingents, and not for coastal defence, as might be expected from the solemn assurance which was given the house. Sir, I am quite within my rights in questioning the assurance given by a minister in that respect.
Will the hon. member permit a question? Against which country is the policy of Canada, in terms of offensive action, directed?

That is the question I
have been asking the government, and to which we have not yet received a satisfactory answer.

I am in agreement with the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) when he says that bombing planes are offensive weapons of war, and I base this assertion upon the statement made last year by the Prime Minister of Great Britain when speaking in the House of Commons at London. The hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. Ross) also made that clear when he said that aeroplanes were weapons that could be used in retaliation; that their specific defensive use was for reprisal purposes.
As I said before, I do not believe that Canada is in danger of attack from the air. Under present conditions I do not think that such an attack would be feasible from a military point of view. Apparently the Department of National Defence and certain members of this house do not agree with that. If these estimates were for the purpose of protecting our women and children instead of buying bombing planes for retaliatory measures, we should be considering ways and means of protecting our people from possible attacks from the air.
Last night reference was made in a Canadian radio commission broadcast to the matter of defensive preparation from air attacks and

to a report issued by a group of Cambridge scientists dealing with the matter. It happened that a copy of this report came to me from Great Britain through the mail last evening. A distinguished group of Cambridge scientists examined the measures that might be taken as protection against attack from the air, and arrived at the conclusion that no absolute protection was possible. Because of that, they are opposed to this form of warfare- to war itself. Among the group is to be found some of the most distinguished scientists at the university of Cambridge. The group includes:
J. D. Bernal, M.A., assistant director of research in crystallography.
H. A. Harris, M.A., D.Se., professor of anatomy.
A. F. W. Hughes, M.A., Ph.D.
Joseph Needham, Sc.D., Sir William Dunn, reader in bio-chemistry.
N. W. Pirie, M.A., Ph.D., demonstrator in bio-chemistry.
J. S. Turner, M.A., Ph.D., demonstrator in botany.
D.	H. Valentine, M.A., demonstrator in botany.
E.	B. Verney, M.A., M.B., B.Ch., F.R.C.P.,
F.R.S., Shield reader in pharmacology.
C. H. Waddington, M.A., lecturer in zoology.
Arthur Walton, ALA., Ph.D.
W. A. Wooster, M.A., Ph.D., lecturer in the department of mineralogy and petrology.
There is a further list of other scientists comprising the group whose names I will not read. They indicate quite clearly the position in which nations taking measures of a provocative nature will find themselves. In my opinion nations that provide air and naval bases are provoking attacks by other nations. As we know, there is no defence from air attacks except retaliation. The question asked a few moments ago by the hon. member for Vancouer North has never been answered in this chamber. He asked: Against whom are we arming, and whom are we preparing to attack? If these estimates were in reality defence estimates, if the department and hon. members of this house believed that we were in danger of air attacks, the thing to do would be not to buy bombing planes but to build bomb-proof and gas-proof shelters for our people in our congested' centres and to teach them the proper measures to take in the event of attack by air. This is not my own conclusion; I am simply repeating the conclusions arrived at among others by the group of scientists referred to in the broadcast last evening. I regard their statement as one of the most authoritative that has been issued. Moreover, they say that there is no protection for children from air attacks.

Against whom does the hon. member protect himself when he locks his door?

Supply-Defence-Air Force
Against the robber or burglar who may be in the vicinity of my home.
Name him.
I say against the robber who may be in the vicinity of my home.
There are many international robbers.
I ask the hon. member what robber is in the vicinity of Canada at the present time and against whom are we preparing these weapons?
Name yours first.
I should like to read from the report to which I just referred.
Scientists will never solve this question.

The following is an article which appeared in The Lancet of December 19, 1936:
Major Blackmore said little could be done for the child under five. From that age on, they could be persuaded to wear a respirator, but the resistance to breathing, though reduced to two and a half inches, was enough to inhibit small children. A pram cover has been designed to convert the perambulator into a gas proof room, and this worked excellently. The objections were the difficulty of manipulating a perambulator, and the fact that only 25 per cent of the population of the east end of London possessed perambulators.
(Melfort): Does that article refer to conditions in Canada or to conditions in another country?
The city of Montreal is probably just as crowded as the city of Liverpool.
But there is more space around it to which the people could be removed,
I imagine that gas would kill the people of Montreal just about as quickly as it would kill the people of Manchester.
But I would point out that they do not have to stay in the city.

I quote further:
A gas-proof box had been designed for children under two and worked well, but the babies objected strongly and yelled. The sight of a mottled face through a yellow celluloid window always convinced the mother that the child was being suffocated and she took it out. Further possibilities were being explored. One of the difficulties was to find personnel for experiment.
And Major Blackmore is in charge of this particular work for the present government of Great Britain. The point I am making is this: 31111-731
We have heard a great deal in this house about the defence of our women and children. Today we are told that we need bombing planes for protection, for retaliatory measures if you will, but no appropriations are to be found in these estimates for giving any real defence for our women and children in the event of air raids. I say, Mr. Chairman, that these defence estimates can be construed only as offence estimates.
In your opinion.

In my opinion. If we are looking for real defence for our people we should examine the scientific factors that will be brought to bear in the next war. If we believe that war is a possibility we should prepare ourselves for that. The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) last night mentioned the new bombs that have been perfected, the thermite bombs. I wonder whether the Department of National Defence has given any consideration to precautions which might be taken to meet the havoc and devastation that would be caused by aeroplanes dropping thermite bombs. There is not a chemical known that will extinguish fires started by that type of bomb because it burns without air. If hon. gentleman care to get the report to which I have referred this afternoon, they will find experiments in the use of thermite described therein, one of which was the dropping of thermite through a pail of water which resulted in burning out the bottom of the pail. To guard against the effect of aerial attacks would be a real defence measure. If we are buying planes because we fear air raids, then I say that the methods of defence which we should adopt are rather methods that would enable us to defend ourselves against the effects of the raids about which we are being continually frightened. I am asking the department to be logical. I have been logical. I have opposed this estimate because I do not believe we are likely to be attacked from the air. I ask the department to be equally logical, and if they believe that air raids upon us are possible, let them make some recommendations to this committee to meet the situation that would then arise, we will say, in a city like Montreal, Halifax, Vancouver or Saint John.

Mr. Chairman, I have not said a word upon these estimates so far, but when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) suggests that the only possible defence for the Dominion of Canada is a gas-bag, a fire hose and a funk hole, I must ask permission to make a brief reply.
You will recall, sir, that in 1914 there was a war. At that time the German cruiser

Supply-Defence-Air Force
Emden broke loose, and raided and sank thousands of tons of British shipping. Perhaps the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, or if he is not a naval or military expert, perhaps the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) can tell us what would have prevented the Emden, had it chosen to do so, from coming to Victoria, destroying the shipping there, passing on to Vancouver and repeating the same process there. Had we anything to defend ourselves with at that time? Was there a man, was there a ship, was there a plane which could have interfered? Am I right when I suggest that the defence upon which we relied at that time was two or three Japanese cruisers which happened by chance to be in the immediate vicinity? I am not a warrior. I do not want war; I deplore war as much as anybody in this house can possibly deplore it, but I submit that we must consider realities.
In 1914 there was also the cruiser squadron of von Spee attacking shipping in the south Atlantic. It met the ships of Cradock, defeated them and then moved towards the east coast of South America. That was a much greater menace than the Emden. What was there to prevent it from going up to Victoria or to the Atlantic ports? Could my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence state that we now have at Vancouver or Victoria or any other coast city, aeroplanes or antiaircraft guns with which one might stop such a squadron from attacking our ports? It is true that the squadron moved around the other way and there was met by a British squadron, but it is conceivable that in the next war conditions might not be exactly the same. It might be that British squadrons will not be .moving freely here and there in the Atlantic to chase German cruisers. History repeats itself, but not always on the same lines. It might be that for a time British warships would be compelled to remain near home and they might have to let a stray vessel of the enemy cross the seas, destroying what it will.
I ask my hon. friends, the military and naval experts in the southeast corner, this question:	Are you willing to say that this
country should go absolutely without defence? I answer that you are not, because you voted this afternoon time and time again for the expenditure of the same amount as we expended last year. You believe in defence, but you do not believe in efficient defence. You believe in fighting, but you believe in fighting with what someone has described as wooden guns. I want peace. I will do anything that is possible for peace. I have asked

this house, and especially the Minister of Finance, and I have appealed to the nation as a whole, that we ought to consider means of expanding our trade and developing our commerce with other nations of the world. But if you are not going to do that, are you going to face realities? Are you going to meet the exigencies of war, as you must do if war comes? Are you going to realize that in that case you must be prepared to defend Canada? And what are you going to defend it with?
I do not suggest to-day that these estimates are too high or too low. I am not competent to judge. All I say is that we have police forces in our cities. Will you withdraw the police? Would the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar who knows someone in his immediate neighbourhood who might be a robber hesitate to lock his door because he did not happen to be acquainted with the robber? I submit that we do not know the nation against which we may be engaged. The scene changes rapidly, and no one knows what may happen. But I want to mention one word that I received to-day in a letter from a friend in London. He said: "My friends here expect the storm to break before July.1' I hope he is wrong. I feel in my heart he must be wrong.
Hear, hear.

I do not believe the world can be so mad. Would we not ourselves be full of madness if we failed to take cognizance of the circumstances, if we failed to realize that when the storm breaks, we may in some measure be brought into close contact with it. When that storm comes, it may be necessary for us to do something, and we at least ought to be prepared, not for every eventuality, but surely for some.

Mr. Chairman, the
hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), whether he intended it or not, has really diverted the discussion from the point we were raising. He urges that we face realities. That is what some of us are trying to do. We are asking whether this greatly increased armament is adequate. The minister cannot say that it is. We are asking against whom are we preparing to fight. The minister cannot name the nation.

Any nation which may be
at war with us.

The minister and
the government are not facing the realities of the situation. If we venture to criticize anything, someone sneers that we are not military and naval experts. Hon. members

Supply-Defence-Air Force
who do the sneering are themselves not much more military and naval experts than anyone else in the committee. We have asked the minister again and again with regard to the advice of experts, but we are told that he must not divulge military secrets and strategy. I submit that although we members of parliament are not naval and military experts and make no pretence of being such, we are called upon again and again in the discussion of estimates to determine upon policies with regard to agriculture, as to which most of us are not experts, with regard to commerce, concerning which most of us are not experts, with regard to labour, with regard to legal matters, in which most of us are not experts. Then why should it be that the military estimates should be considered as quite different from any other? Though we may not be military experts, some of us have been trained in some degree in logic, and logical reasoning is not confined to either side of this house or any group in this house. As duly elected representatives we are asked to determine upon a certain policy, and it does not help to clear the situation When hon. members opposite sneer or pound their desks.
The hon. member for Huron North had a good deal to say about guns and ships and anti-aircraft. I submit that the vote we are discussing is not concerned with any of these things.
Why not?

What we are now concerned with is planes, bombing planes. It is curious that although the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) objected to this provision on the ground that essentially it would mean offensive rather than defensive warfare, the minister had nothing to say. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) supplemented what had been said earlier by quoting an authoritative statement, from men who are dealing with this very question at close quarters in England. Again, the minister has nothing to say in rebuttal of the argument. Only a few minutes ago an hon. member who sits just behind the minister distinctly made the statement, in supporting the government's policy, that bombing planes were practically useless except for retaliation. The minister has not indicated whether he accepts such supporting opinions as that. From all I have read, it is generally agreed that bombing planes are of very little value except as a means of retaliation. Yet the minister has nothing to say when we point to an argument of that kind, an argument put forward as one reason for supporting the estimate for an increased expenditure
on bombing planes. When, a few days ago, we were urged to accept these increased estimates and all that this program involves, we asked against whom we were arming. We pointed out that it was next to impossible for the Japanese on one coast or the Germans on the other to send an expedition to Canada. We were told in reply that occasionally raiders may come over here and that we ought to be able to repel occasional raids from whatever country they come. One would have thought that if we were facing realities the program would be one of coastal defence. Quite true, certain increases along that line have been proposed, but now the minister comes along with proposals for an increased expenditure well on to seven millions of dollars, the major part of which relates to this arm of defence, and we ask the reason for it. It is admitted that if a raider came across at this time, our bombing planes would not be much good, but the major purpose of the bombing plane would be retaliation. Let us come to realities. Is it suggested that if a German plane, we will say, came over here and managed, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) put it the other day, to drop a bomb on a granary in Saskatchewan, we must send our air force away over the Atlantic to drop bombs on Germany?
No.
That is the logic of the proposal.
To protect us against such an attack.

Are we to understand that our only purpose in providing for such a large force of aeroplanes circling over this country or known to be somewhere available, is that the Germans will be afraid to come over here for fear that we then would go over to Germany? I suggest we are being driven to extreme and imaginary assumptions if that is the argument in support of the vote. Is it possible for us to accept that point of view without going contrary to the policy which we have been assured is the policy of this government? I could hardly but accept the statements of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), coming as they did from men who are sincere. I could hardly but accept the assurance they gave the other day that this defence vote was for purely defence purposes. But, Mr. Chairman, whatever they may think, I do not know exactly the means by which advice is passed on from one governmental body to another, from the United Kingdom to this country, but I do say that we have the right to be suspicious. We have the

Supply-Defence-Air Force
right to be suspicious when, we find that a major part of the increase is to be devoted, not to defence purposes-admittedly it would be useless for strictly defence purposes-but to what would be of value as a means of retaliation. That retaliation would undoubtedly carry our planes over to some foreign country. Again and again it has been admitted that we are not going to attack the United States. Then the only other foreign country would be overseas.. It may be that somewhere there will be a submarine upon which a bomb might be dropped. I admit that possibility. But essentially that would not deter a great nation from sending bombers over to this country. The effective use of bombers can mean only that we would send bombing planes to Europe or to Asia, and that means that we depart entirely from the policy which the Minister of Justice, the Prime Minister, and the Minister of National Defence himself have stated is the policy of Canada. I think we ought to be fair in this matter.

Hear,
hear.
I think we ought to be straightforward in this matter..
Hear, hear.

I am glad to hear the minister say, "hear, hear." Then the government should proceed with perfect fairness and frankness. Somebody said that the Minister of National Defence had laid all his cards on the table. I am not suggesting that he has some Machiavellian plan to put this program over on Canada, but I do suggest to him that the program which is being outlined is not one that will commend itself to a very great number of Canadians as being a purely defence program. And that is especially true of this item. It has been charged in some sections of the chamber that we in this corner have not been absolutely consistent. I do not know what other course we could have taken in order to be consistent. We have from the very first opposed the increase in armaments, and we are opposing it item by item. When our motion of lack of confidence was before the house, the Prime Minister suggested that we had some other end in view and that when it came to the estimates we would not vote against them. That was his suggestion in opposing our resolution. Well, we are voting against these increases steadily, item by item, and we propose to continue doing so; we are sincere in that. Some of us believe that we could settle the matter far better by other means than by
{Mr. Woodsworth.]
military defence preparations. I am convinced of the truth of that. As I tried to set forth in my resolution earlier in the session, I believe that if, in an endeavour to bring about better relations between Canada and the other countries, if necessary making financial sacrifices and refusing to ship our raw materials to be used in the manufacture of armaments in other countries, thus provoking yet other countries to retaliation,-if to that end we devoted one-tenth of the attention and one-tenth of the money that we give to military matters, it would be a surer defence than any other which could be provided. I have said that again and again. I should like to wipe out all these increases. But an item of this kind is particularly objectionable, simply because it seems to indicate that, if not in the back of the minister's mind, at any rate in the back of the minds of his officials-and we have no way of getting at them except through the minister-there is the idea that these military bombing planes may be used not in Canada but for some expedition outside Canada. They are mobile; they are the arm that could be most readily used if we were asked to send a military expedition abroad. One cannot but have the feeling that somewhere considerations of this kind are behind this program.
We are given a picture to-day of what will be involved, and if bombs are dropped in other countries it will be on other households, upon women and children as well as men. I can very well recollect, as can many hon. members, the consternation, the abhorrence, we experienced in the last war when the Germans began using gas. It was a horrible thing, we thought; never would we resort to any such thing. Throughout the world there was an outcry against it. Yet the horror has passed and the use of gas and gas bombs and bombing planes is being accepted as essential in. modern warfare. That is the picture to which we must look forward.
I wish to say as a Canadian-and I feel sure I represent the feeling of tens of thousands of other Canadians-that we would do anything rather than involve this country in fratricidal strife.
Hear, hear.

I think that is
true. I will not sneer at my hon. friends opposite, for I believe they would do almost anything to avoid such a state of affairs. But I do say that they are adopting a military program which will inevitably land us in that sort of thing. They do not want it any more than I do, but they are adopting a program which in the end means war, and not

Supply-Defence-Air Force
merely war for the defence of our own borders but war which will inevitably land us in some foreign country. That is the end of the road.

Does the hon. member
really believe that bombing planes are not used in coastal defence?

The best information that I can secure is, as was stated by an hon. member on the government side a few minutes ago, that bombing planes are almost useless for purely defensive purposes. That is my information.
If the hon. member is referring to me, I object to that statement; I never said any such thing.

Hansard will show
it. He said that bombing was practically useless except as a means of retaliation. I believe that was the meaning of his words. I should not like to do him wrong but that is what I wrote down.
May I ask the hon. member one question? What would he do in the event of an enemy nation sailing aeroplane carriers within a few hours' distance of our coast? What method of offence would he adopt?

I do not think I
am particularly called upon to answer that question. That contingency is so remote that we can very well disregard it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is one question which has been asked so often during the course of this debate, and which I regard as so preposterous, that I consider it my duty to answer it. Hon. gentlemen are asking us: Against whom are you arming? Can there be anything more ludicrous than that question? My hon. friend has just asked the same question, and I ask him: Can he cite any country in the world, any parliament in a civilized country where, when they organize their defence, they broadcast to the world that they are arming against this or that country? It is absurd to ask that question and my hon. friend knows it.
We in Canada are a peaceful people and we try to maintain friendly relations with all the nations of the world. We have no enemies, I hope; in fact I know we have no enemies. How can my hon. friend ask us to say that we are arming against somebody in particular? But we live in a world the conditions in which we cannot ignore. We live in a world which is arming everywhere and in a way we all deplore. At no time in history has there been such intensive arming on the part of every
nation as there is at the present time. Rulers of nations advertise themselves, as was done in two countries which I could name but shall not, as wanting by force to propagate their doctrines throughout the world. As I say, we are the enemy of no one, but we have to take into account the madness that prevails everywhere. And we try at least-at least, I repeat-to defend ourselves in case of need. My hon. friends themselves are voting for credits for defence. Some hon. members on that side, and even on this side, have moved amendments to reduce the items in the estimates, but they want to keep the amounts as they were last year or the year before; that is an admission that there must be some provision for the defence of Canada. If there must be some national defence, is it not proper that it should be at least a little efficient, a little effective? That is a question more logical and reasonable than the one asked by my hon. friend.
After all, the first law of life is that of selfpreservation. Every organism that lives seeks to protect itself, to make conditions so that it may live. The first duty of a nation is to defend its citizens; that I believe, no one will contradict. But my hon. friends say: Oh, we are in no danger, there is no need; we cannot foresee any. Well, to govern is to foresee. On a question like this we cannot follow our own personal fancies; we must take into account our responsibilities for our fellow men in Canada, and if unfortunately in a certain emergency something happens which my hon. friends say cannot happen, but which others say may happen, I could not justify myself to my conscience for neglect to take precautions by saying that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) or the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) or the communist party of Toronto or some groups in my own province told me that we did not need any defence. We are responsible; we have to make provision, and that is what we are doing at this time, as members of the government and as members of parliament doing our duty as God has given us the light to see it. I have heard somebody say: These explanations are all right, but my electors in the sixth range of some township will not understand that. Mr. Chairman, we are not going to govern Canada on that basis. I am a member of this government, and we are going to govern Canada in the way which we believe is the straightforward, honest and fair way for the protection of our citizens. And let me also ask-for some hon. members come back time after time with the suggestion that we are preparing for participation in wars outside Canada-why

Supply-Defence-Air Force
should hon. gentlemen say this when they know that it is not the case, when they know that it is not true-

Mr. Chairman, I
ask that that statement be withdrawn.

It is no worse than the
statement made by the hon. member a few minutes ago. Let him withdraw his own.

Mr. Chairman, on
a point of order. The Minister of Justice said that in expressing ourselves as we had done we made statements which we knew not to be true.
No.
Which we knew to be wrong. I say that statement must be withdrawn.

No. But I have
been in this house for a good many years and I have never seen a member compelled to stop to do that.

speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will be good enough to put his appeal against the ruling of the chair in writing, and present it to the table.

Mr. Chairman, speaking to the point of order, during the twelve years I have been a member I have never seen a motion which was not in writing. speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
In 1935 the provincial legislature of Ontario passed an act respecting the guardianship of the Dionne quintuplets. Under this act the Minister of Public Welfare was appointed a special guardian and the lieutenant governor in council was empowered to appoint additional guardians. At the present time His Honour Judge Valin, Doctor Dafoe and the father, Mr. Dionne, are the active guardians of the quintuplets and in them is vested full power to look after the health and general welfare of the quintuplets.
An application was made recently to the patent office for the registration of the words "quins," "quints" and "quintuplets" as trade marks to be used exclusively in connection with certain articles. The application lists
some two hundred articles, but I shall read only a few. It was made by the Blossom Products Corporation, of Allentown Pennsylvania, in the month of January and asks the right to use these words in connection with panties, bloomers, stepins, undersuits of knitted and woven fabrics, pyjamas, bathing suits, corsets, combinations, slips, mufflers, mittens, knickers, rompers, creepers, ties, bibs, overalls, suspenders, wind-breakers, crossword puzzles, paper games, bicycles, tricycles, brooms, kiddy carts, wheelbarrows, scooters, checker boards, blankets, spreads, beddings, pillows, mattresses, quilts, sheets, scarves, alcoholic beverages, ale, beer, gin, whisky, brandy, dental cream, toothbrushes, lip and cheek rouge, mascara, eye shadow, eyebrow pencil, high chairs, baby chairs, tobaccos, cigarettes, pipes, patent medicines and sewing boxes, in connection with all of which wares the applicant is exclusively concerned. The commissioner of patents found' that he would be bound to grant the application of the applicants unless some protection was given. This bill proposes to vest exclusively in the guardians of the quintuplets the right to use the words "quins," "quints" and "quintuplets." Perhaps hon. members would like to discuss this bill and may have certain suggestions to make by way of amendment, and for these reasons I think it only right, should the house agree, that the bill should be referred to the private bills committee. I have discussed this matter with the commissioner of patents and he advises me that this is the only procedure by which the necessary protection can be given.

Mr. Speaker, as this bill is going
before the private bills committee I shall not discuss it at length at this time. I may say that I claim no experience in this matter, but I wish to confirm what has been said by the sponsor of the bill (Mr. Gray). Unless a bill of this kind is passed, the objects hoped to be attained can not be attained. Under the provisions of the Unfair Competition Act, which is a statute passed in 1932, dealing with the registration of trade marks, generally speaking trade marks in the form of a word may be registered only in association with specific commodities which are manufactured or sold by the person seeking to register the trade mark. On the other hand, there is nothing in the act giving the Secretary of State any discretionary power to refuse an application by any firm for the registration of the word "quintuplets" or other words of that kind. Although this is a common word, it has come to have great commercial value because

The department has always taken the stand that it could not view favourably any legislation which devised to private or commercial firms special privileges, but it would appear that the circumstances in this case are such that the department would not oppose this bill. I venture to say that no such measure has ever before been submitted to any parliament. I wonder whether the house realizes just what this bill means? We are now being asked to call these words trade marks and vest them in the guardians for purposes not at all related to commerce. Just before recess I was about to ask the minister -a question. At the moment, however, I should like to make some observations with reference to remarks by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deach-man), and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to -the effect that we of this group
have hardly been consistent in that we voted for estimates equal to the amount of last year. We have not opposed defence. We have opposed the increase in defence, because we do not believe that any adequate reason has been shown for these increased estimates. The Minister of Justice made a strange remark. He said he did not propose to be convinced that the vote was a waste of money merely because that point of view was advocated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), the communist party in Toronto, and some sections of his own province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is quite true.
I would not go so far as to say that the minister intentionally lumped together all these groups for the purpose of inferring that the inspiration for this opposition came from the communist party.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a mere coincidence.

If such an interpretation should be put upon our action, I should like to state here and now that our opposition has been consistent with the policy and philosophy of this group. While it is not unusual to hear some hon. gentlemen associate us with the communist party, in order to cast somewhat of a slur upon our group, it is unusual to hear them include also any hon. members from Quebec who happen to differ from the government.
I think we are fully within our rights in asking two questions with reference to these increases: first, if they are needed, and, second, if they are to be used exclusively for defence. The minister said this afternoon that the question against whom the provision is to be made is totally irrelevant, because in other countries where rearmament is being voted no mention is made of the nation against whom they are rearming. That is hardly in accordance with the facts. As a matter of fact, again and again in the Japanese diet Russia has been cited as the nation against whom Japan is providing defence. Hitler has stated repeatedly that fear of communism is what causes his country to arm. The Prime Minister of Great Britain made the statement not long ago that the frontier for Great Britain was on the Rhine, and that Britain must protect the sea route to India, which is the life-line of the empire. I think these statements clearly show against whom those nations are arming. But no such statement has been made in connection with these estimates. We are repeatedly

Supply-Defence-Air Force
told that we have no enemies, and at the same time, that we must defend ourselves lest some time or another we should manage to develop enemies. There is no reason for some of the indignation that was displayed this afternoon merely because we asked, quite frankly, are these purchases that it is now proposed to make, in the best interests of defence, or are they such as will not give adequate defence but rather will lend themselves to the formation of a mobile unit for use elsewhere? In asking the minister to give that information, we are not being obstructionists, nor are we trying to be facetious. Therefore I ask the minister just what part would bombing planes play in actual defence in the event either of an attack by raiders or an invasion of our coasts.

This is the first time during the discussion of these estimates that the minister in charge of them has been asked this question by any member of the group in the corner. All the members of the group other than the hon. member who has just spoken took it for granted, and so stated plainly in this committee, that these estimates were to be used for offensive purposes outside the Dominion of Canada, and they thereby broke the rules of the house, because not only my leader, the Prime Minister, but two or three of our colleagues and many others who are conversant with the policy underlying these estimates stated, not once, but time after time on the floor of the house that not one cent of these estimates is intended for any purposes of aggression outside Canada, but that the vote is intended solely for the defence of the dominion. I think my friends and my political opponents alike will agree with me that I have refrained from any provocative utterances during the discussion of these estimates. What has happened? My hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation moved an amendment when Mr. Speaker was in the chair a week ago. The debate upon that amendment occupied the house for almost a week. During the discussion unequivocal assurances were given by the government that every cent of these estimates-air force, militia and naval estimates-was for the defence of Canada, of Canadian territorial waters and Canadian neutrality. Yet when we come to the items, hon. member after hon. member day after day rises in his place and refuses to accept the assurances which have been given. There is a rule that when an hon. member rises in his place and makes a statement his word is to be accepted, and I am very much surprised at the suspicion and distrust which

seem to have been engendered in the minds of my hon. friends opposite.
With reference to the use of bombing planes, I do not pretend to the wonderful knowledge that some of my critics appear to have, but the best technical advice I have received is that the most effective defensive weapon to-day is the aeroplane, the bombing aeroplane. My hon. friends, however, will not accept the assurances of those who give this technical advice. I desire again to assure the hon. member for Weyburn, if assurance is of any use to him, that every cent of these estimates is intended for the purposes that have been specified, for the defence of Canada.
I asked the minister a perfectly civil question. I hardly think it is necessary-

We muit not give to our Canadian boys, the finest fighters in the air the world 'has ever seen, decent aeroplanes to meet anyone who might assail us. That is the policy of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I have never seen such inconsistency, suspicion and mistrust in all my experience in the House of Commons.
I asked a question, and I am still waiting for the answer. I enjoyed the exuberant eloquence of the hon. gentleman,, but I should like to get an answer to the question which I asked.

The
question was with regard to bombing aeroplanes, and the answer is that according to the best opinion they constitute one of the most effective defensive weapons.
The minister accuses the group over here of holding up the estimates and prolonging the debate.
Oh, no.

Oh, yes, he did. He said that day after day this discussion had gone on in the house, and he also accused us of being responsible for the debate which took place during the best part of last week. They were the ones who took up the time. And the same thing with regard to the amendments. The items under discussion yesterday and again to-day have been spoken to mostly by members on the minister's side. I do not know of any member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group that has moved any amendments; possibly one may have done so. Most of the amendments came from supporters of the minister himself. Why, therefore, does he accuse us? As the hon. member for Weyburn said, his own exuberance ran away with him and he forgot himself, and possibly the same remark applies to some of the arguments he has used. I have not spoken a great deal on the question. I asked a few questions for information and I do not believe any of us in this group are entirely
