opposed to having defence. I realize that we must have some defence, just as it was pointed out that if we are to preserve order in any community, we must have the nucleus of a police force there. But there is legitimate room for differences of opinion on these estimates. I am of opinion that we could have had the same efficiency in connection with the defence forces of the country with the amount of money spent last year as we shall have with the money we are asked to vote on this occasion.
Give the basis of your opinion.

It is my opinion though
it may not be worth much, and in a discussion such as this I do not suppose that it would be worth much, but I believe the opinion is shared by many others. As I have said here before, if only a tithe of this money spent for war purposes were spent in an effort to foster peace sentiments among the nations, we should get far more value for the money expended than we receive for the money spent on munitions and in preparing for some eventuality.

The Minister of National Defence is greatly concerned about the inconsistency of the defence policies of the small group in this corner, but I am not sure that his own party are all at one on their defence policy. There is possibly more inconsistency on that side, not only relatively, but perhaps on the whole. When he has got rid of the inconsistency in his own camp, he can come over here and lecture us. Let us look at the situation we were dealing with last Thursday. I made some reference to sanctions-and remember sanctions were applied by the Liberal government against Italy in 'the war with Ethiopia. If those sanctions had led to war, would the government have taken part in that war or would they have backed out? That is a question we have a right to ask the government.

Why don't you ask
us where the fire goes when it goes out?

Judging by the look of
distress on the hon. member's face, I doubt whether he himself knows the answer to that. The question before the dominion is Still the question of foreign policy and we have not settled it yet, nor have we done anything towards settling it. Am I to understand, is the bouse to understand, is the country to understand, that in developing this defence policy we are withdrawing from the League of Nations and will take no further part in applying sanctions or in any other

phase of the work of the league? That is a question which must be answered satisfactorily to the people of Canada. If we are going to withdraw, what alignments are we going to make? One of these alternatives is inevitable; which one are we going to choose?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When I spoke on a previous occasion, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar asked me whether I would make a statement of our foreign policy. In that statement of our foreign policy I drew the attention of the house to the fact that the policy of the government with respect to sanctions was to allow parliament to decide. That was a clear statement and it was accepted by everybody.

The Minister of National Defence paid some attention to some remarks I made both last night and to-day with regard to what constitutes real defence against air attacks. I am not retracting anything I said in that regard. It may be called in derision a national policy of dug-outs, but I fancy that if the hon. gentleman will read Hansard and see what I actually said and the views I expressed, together with the authorities upon which I based those views, he will feel ashamed of that remark. If we are really in danger of attack, as the minister has constantly reminded us, I wanted to see that the women and children for whose protection these armaments are supposed to be obtained, shall be provided with some defences. And there is nothing in these estimates that will provide any such defence.
My point of view regarding armaments can be well stated in the words which I read in the debate of a week ago yesterday. I suppose there was no man in the British Empire more closely associated with the foreign policy of Great Britain in the pre-

Supply

Defence-Air Force
war years than the late Sir Edward Grey. Shortly after the beginning of the war, Sir Edward Grey used these words:
The increase of armaments that is intended in each nation to produce consciousness of strength and a sense of security does not produce these effects.
On the contrary, it produces the consciousness of strength of other nations and a sense of fear. The enormous growth of armaments in Europe, the sense of insecurity and fear caused by them-it was these that made war inevitable.
This statement, I believe, is absolutely correct. Last week we saw the announcement from Great Britain of a great armament program, and a day or two later there was a discussion in Germany regarding the matter, and a sense of greater insecurity engendered there. The result will be that Germany will adopt another great armament program. That will cause Russia to build up still greater armaments, and so the mad race goes on, until the time comes when one nation feels that it is in a position to bring the matter to a show-down. It is a tragedy for the world that collective security has broken down. I would be glad to see a reconstituted and reorganized League of Nations, with some power such as an international police force to enforce law and order in the world. But these individual national rearmament programs can lead only to ruin and chaos, and that is the reason for my opposition to these estimates. I have consistently preached this for years. What I have said in this house is what I have said ever since the war. And I am not in the position of some hon. gentlemen who perhaps did not make their position clear prior to the election. I did. And I had many friends among hon. gentlemen opposite who told me that I was not alone in that attitude, that it was the policy of the Liberal party. Consequently, when I see this rearmament program proceeding, I feel, rightly or wrongly, but conscientiously at least, that I must oppose it. Because I agree with the statement made by Sir Edward Grey when the war broke out, that a sense of insecurity will pervade the world and all the nations, it also seems to me that we in this part of the world, small in population, with a tremendous territory to protect, ought to weigh well the consequences of joining in such a race and of following a policy which may appear provocative. The item under discussion, that of bombing planes, is a provocative item. The Minister of National Defence and those advising him may believe that bombing planes constitute an arm of defence; I do not, nor, may I add, do those who have spoken of aeroplanes in the British House of Commons, including the Prime Minister of Great Britain. So we in this group are opposing these increased estimates because we believe they can lead only to further rearmament and to ultimate disaster. When the minister complains about obstructionist tactics, let me point out, as was done by my colleague from Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps), that last week only five of this group spoke, for forty minutes each or less. But the debate went on all week. None of the group to my immediate right spoke; almost the entire debate was carried on by the supporters of the government. When I used to read Hansard before I came here, I marvelled how the present Minister of National Defence, when he was in opposition, could manage to keep up such a barrage on the ministers who were then in power. Consequently, it comes with rather poor grace from the minister that he should complain that we are examining these estimates thoroughly.
I did not complain.
Then what was all the heat about?
It was all light.

No, I never said that.
Well, if I am mistaken, I am glad to withdraw the reflection upon the minister.
May I ask a question of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken? Sometimes I may use provocative language-
Oh, no, no!

-especially when through the chair I reply to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan). But my hon. friend who has just spoken said that this increase is a provocation. They had just been completed under the direction of some of the greatest French and British engineers, when the great war broke out. Belgium was destroyed. I look at Denmark, and I see it practically unarmed when the war began.
A different thing, altogether.
Not now.

It had the most desirable naval bases for operation against the British navy which could be found on the Shores of the North sea. But Denmark was not invaded, because she provided no excuse

no provocation, if you like-for invasion. That is my view.

speechtext: To what extent was Canada armed before the last war?
Canada was not well armed before the great war, but Canada entered that war of her own volition.
And she will the next.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to change the subject for a moment, and get on a peace-time footing. I understand the plans of the Department of National Defence call for certain extensions at the Jericho air base in Vancouver. There is some suggestion that part of the extension will require taking over a portion of Locarno park, which adjoins the base, on the west. May I point out that the park is comparatively small, but that it is one of the most popular parks in Vancouver, has one of the safest bathing beaches for children and is one of the best parks for picnic purposes. It would be too bad if the department were to take over any of the park, because I believe in the vicinity there is vacant land which should be used, even if it is not quite so satisfactory. I suggest that the minister give the matter serious consideration before any of the park area is taken over.

The question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South is one of negotiation at the

present time with the Vancouver city council and the Vancouver parks board. No decision has yet been reached; the matter is still under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, may I call the attention of the minister to the fact that Fredericton, the capital city in the province of New Brunswick, has no air port. In a defence program it would surely be regarded proper to have a landing field at each capital city, and I would ask that consideration be given to providing one for Fredericton.
Representations have been received from New Brunswick, and the matter is now under consideration.

The vote in question involves a large sum of money, and I do not believe the minister fully answered the question I put to him. I know he has had a grilling for two days, and perhaps he is a little irascible. But in asking him as to the usefulness of bombing planes for defence purposes, I do not think we are casting any aspersions on the word of the Prime Minister or on that of the Minister of Justice.
The aspirations of ministers are always dangerous.

I was talking about aspersions, not aspirations. Emerson said: "Your actions speak so loudly I can't hear what you say." The only way we can judge the use to which any arm of the service will be put is to know the nature of that part of the service. I can imagine that a bombing plane might be used to attack an aircraft carrier or, in a remote instance, perhaps to attack a submarine, although depth charges would seem to be the logical weapon for that purpose. If there are any other uses, I think the officials should give them to us, through the minister. That is the only way we can judge whether the major part of this great sum of money is going to be used in a service which will actually constitute a defence, or whether it will be used for other purposes. I think that is a fair question.

I believe I replied to the question on at least two occasions. As I said, out of the 102 aeroplanes involved in the estimates, only 24 are bombing planes. As I said this afternoon, there are other types such as fighters, reconnaissance, torpedo bombers, bombers and also small training planes, which constitute 27 out of the total of 102. In the opinion of those whose advice is competent, bombing planes

Supply-Defence-Air Force
are most effective, with fighter and reconnaissance planes, for defensive purposes. That is as clear, as lucid and as precise as I can make my answer.

One other question-and this is the last: If I understood him correctly the minister said this afternoon that some of the planes were being built in England because the British air ministry thought it wise to have planes of the same design and make. Is that correct?

No, it
is not exactly correct. The reason they were made in England previously was that we did not have resources in Canada for building them. Deliveries from England of some planes ordered have taken about twenty-four months, before they have actually reached Canada. So the hon. member can see that if there are immediate requirements-and there are

we must look to other sources for the production of the planes.

Did I understand the
minister to say that it was desirable to have planes of the same design as those in the British air force?
Yes, certainly.
Why? What is the object of that?

Because it has been for many years the considered policy in all arms of the service that equipment in all branches shall be of a pattern identical with that used by the mother country if possible. That is the reason.

Mr. Chairman, I have a number of questions to ask in connection with this estimate which I think is of sufficient importance to warrant questions being asked and their being answered. I fail to understand why this group should have ricidule and sarcasm heaped upon it because its members view this matter very seriously. I think I have a right to view this matter seriously as I have a distinct recollection of many hour? of the time of this parliament being spent on subjects of less consequence, on matters of a, purely partisan and political nature. If we make a mistake in formulating a national policy, it may mean the lives of many Canadian young men. Of 'that there can be no doubt. We stand at an important point in our national affairs and there is little excuse for the levity which has been assumed by some members. While in the heat of debate provocative remarks may be passed, I do not think hon. members should question our sincerity. I think they should recognize that we are accorded the support of many thousands of our fellow citizens.
The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) brought up a matter which has not yet been satisfactorily answered. The minister stated that he was relying almost implicitly upon the expert advice of the departmental staff. He suggested that we were questioning the good faith of himself and of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in giving certain assurances to this house. I do not intend to suggest for one moment that the Prime Minister or the Minister of National Defence has attempted to deceive this committee. I think the Minister of National Defence must admit that both he and his deputy minister, a man for whom we all have the greatest esteem, are so burdened with administrative details that they cannot give the necessary study to questions of a technical nature. The minister has admitted quite frankly that he must rely upon this expert advice.
The minister asks that we rely upon the advice of men who during the past eighteen years have received from this parliament approximately $300,000,000. That vast amount has been expended by these experts, and yet

Supply-Defence-Air Force
the Minister of National Defence rose in his place the other evening and said that at the present time we have no defence, that we must ignore all t'he activities of the past and start anew. This is the same staff of experts whose advice must now be accepted by this house.
It was shown very clearly that the most ghastly and stupid blunders were made by the general Staff at the outbreak of the last war. They said that bombs could not possibly be used in trench warfare, that the private soldier would have to rely upon rifles and bayonets. It was Tommy Atkins himself who discovered that if he was in a hole here and Heinie was in a hole over there, he could take a jam tin, fill it with guncotton and a few rusty nails and get at his enemy. That is what was done in spite of the advice of the experts on the general staff. The history of the general staff has been that of retarding development. We have in the evidence of the Minister of National Defence clear proof of the incompohency of the present staff, upon whose advice we must rely. The minister should not seek to answer our questions by stating that that is the best advice possible.
I think the experience in the last war was such as to give us the right to suggest that the general staff in Canada is acting in rather too close cooperation with the British War Office. The general atmosphere of the Department of National Defence is such as to suggest that they rely almost entirely upon the advice of the experts of the British War Office. It is quite reasonable to suspect that similar conditions exist to-day as existed at the outbreak of the last war when it was found that commitments, of which the British government had no knowledge, had been made in the name of the British Empire.
The minister alleged that this group was inconsistent because the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) stated that he would participate in a war in defence of collective security. I should like to point out one phase of that question which has not been dealt with. Under a genuine system of collective security, national increases in armaments would not be necessary. The genuine assertion of a policy of collective security without increased armaments would mean an overwhelming superiority of pooled armaments which would make increased armaments individually unnecessary. It is the abandonment of the policy of collective security and the resorting to a policy of individual rearming which has led us on our present mad course. I think these points should be borne in mind. The minister in his estimates this afternoon dealt with the increase in personnel in the

Mr. Chairman, as I have not so far spoken on these estimates, I cannot be accused of taking up the time of the committee, nor am I going to speak very long tonight. So much has been said from different sides on this question that it is very conflicting, I think, to almost everyone of us. I should like to put the question from another angle for a few moments.
We are told that the world has gone mad. Surely it is time for us to restore a little sanity somewhere. I have been thinking along this line: We are voting this session for defence purposes around 835,000,000. Suppose Canada, for instance, said: As a government we shall try a new experiment in the world.

We shall cut out absolutely all armaments, defence or otherwise; we shall use that money in the production of the necessities of life in this country, and then we shall distribute these necessities of life among those countries that need them most. If we have an enemy, we shall give them that which they need, and the keener the enemy the more goods we shall give them. I am just wondering what
834,000,000 or $35,000,000 would mean to Canada if it were used in the extra production of goods to be distributed among other nations. I am wondering what effect this would have on the nation which received these goods as a free gift. I hope the day is not far distant, when some nation.-and I hope it will be one of the leading nations-will have the courage to take such action.
I am thinking of a Teacher of a long while ago who laid down certain rides for the government of mankind, and I think the nation that first adopts the golden rule will be the foremost and most respected nation in the world. I say again, think of what that $34,000,000 would mean to Canada if it were used in our mines, in our manufactures, on our farms and so on. A little while ago we had a tremendous surplus of wheat. Would it not have been a fine gesture to have given that wheat to the country that needed it most? I repeat, it is said that the world is gone mad. Let us try to bring back a little sanity by applying the golden rule. That will solve problems both national and international.

There is one point the minister has not so far mentioned which ought to be recalled; it is that in arranging for the contingents which are to take part in the ceremonies, there has been conference between the different dominions, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Canada, and as far as it has been possible to do so, an arrangement has been worked out for representation in relation to the size
[Mr. I. Mackenzie.!
of the dominions. I believe it is true, relatively speaking that other countries in the empire, having regard to size, are sending larger representations than Canada. What should be kept in mind is that so far as these coronation ceremonies are concerned the eyes of the world will be upon the different dominions represented there. There will be seen on the screen, in all the theatres in different parts of the empire, views of those who took part in the ceremonies. The whole coronation will be broadcast from one end of the world to the other. All that the government is seeking to do is to have Canada hold her place relatively with the other dominions in these proceedings.

May I offer a suggestion
that would make for economy? I will not reduce the number of men. But the transportation overseas represents a large amount. I remember distinctly that at the time of the Gaspe tricentennial celebration the Prime Minister of Canada very wisely went down from Montreal to Gaspe on the Saguenay. We have two boats now, the Saguenay and the Vancouver. I wonder whether, for the last time that they are in service for the Dominion of Canada, it would not be proper to use those boats for something definite before we scrap them. They served once for

Supply-Defence-Coronation
the Prime Minister of Canada to go to Gaspe, we should use them to carry our delegation to the coronation. This would mean a saving of $60,000. I propose no amendment, but I make that suggestion to the minister. What was good enough for the then Prime Minister of Canada must be good enough for any member of the delegation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are obsolete ships, and we are not obsolete.

The Minister of Justice,
I hope, will not lead a regiment there, although he is the head of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Would the minister be kind enough to tell the committee who led the Canadian representation to the coronation of His late Majesty King George Y, and whether that officer was a member of the House of Commons?
I believe the selection made at that time was the senior combatant acting officer of the House of Commons, Colonel Maclean.

I suppose that in this matter, as in the other items of expenditure, the government have definitely made up their mind, and that this vote will be passed, but I must once more protest against this large expenditure for such a purpose. Canada in the past has not been a military nation. It seems we are now in danger of becoming militarized. There are these ceremonies connected with the coronation of the king. With what other nations of the empire may have done or may propose to do I am not very much concerned; I am thinking of Canada and what she should do. Evidently we are making the coronation very largely an occasion for military display. Evidently there is, even in this minor matter, an arrangement among the different dominions. I suppose it will exhibit the solidarity of the empire from a military standpoint; every nation outside the British commonwealth will interpret it in that way. I do not think that is a good impression to go abroad, if we propose to restrict our military activities to our own defence. If the coronation of the king is an event in which all the population of this country aTe supposed to take an interest, I do not know why those who go should be limited to members of parliament, public officials and particularly the military. The suggestion may be regarded as fantastic, but I made it the other night and I repeat it, that since the vast majority of the people of Canada who have built up this country are farmers, labour men, business
men, there is no earthly reason why farmers and labour men and business men should not be sent to the coronation. But that is not being done. I can understand that they might feel very much out of place in the blaze of colour which no doubt the papers will report at the time of the coronation. But such people are the basis of our Canadian life, and I do not see why we should elevate one particular class in this country and give them a joy-ride while other people remain at home. Those who remain at home, the farmers moiling and toiling across the western plains, the labouring people, are going to pay the bills. There is no one else to pay them. If the minister proposed to insist that the very wealthy, and those easily able to pay, should bear the entire cost, one could not make quite as strong an objection, but the cost is distributed over the entire population, poor as well as rich. It is, however, only one class of the community which has any part in the celebrations. It is no wonder that great numbers of the people in this country begin to doubt whether the government as it now exists is in reality a government of the people, and whether they should take any particular interest in the coronation ceremonies.
I wyish to point out, as my colleagues have done, that we have very needy cases in this dominion. Almost every post brings to my desk, as I am sure it does to many others, appeals for help, statements of the desperate conditions existing in Canada. I am thinking not merely of personal appeals for help, but of appeals on behalf of large groups of people. We have nearly a million people on relief; that is just one group, a very important one. It is all very well for the government to say: Oh, well, under the British North America Act we cannot do anything about it, or we can do only this much, we can give grants in aid. Simply to screw such unfortunate people down to bare existence, while other classes in the community are given every opportunity, is not right; it is not consonant with the principles of democracy. I protest against that kind of thing. We have the money in hand to do things like this, but we have not the money to help these needy people. We are told we should protect the mothers and the children, but we read daily of the pressing needs of mothers and children in every, province of this country, lacking ordinary medical necessities, in many cases not supplied even with sufficient food, and yet we have these vast expenditures for purposes of ostentation. If we must have soldiers go abroad, cut this contingent in two and cut the expenses in two, and I am quite sure that the people of this

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is very hard to satisfy my hon, friend, and I am not surprised that he has seized this new opportunity of making some capital politically. But may I tell my hon. friend this: the king is going to be crowned in London, and for the first time as King of Canada. Instead of being crowned in Ottawa or Cape Town or Canberra or Sydney or Melbourne or any of the other capitals of the nations of the commonwealth, he is being crowned in London, and there he takes the oath to govern his people in Canada, his people in New Zealand, his people in Australia. If, instead of having the present arrangement, we had a king or a. ruler who would be crowned in Canada I should like to know whether we could get away with
S197.000.	If, instead of having a monarchy, we had a republic, as some irresponsible people mention at times, do we think we could get away with $197,000? Does the hon. member believe there would be nobody dressed in military uniforms if, instead of being a nation in the British commonwealth of nations, participating in the coronation of our king in London. we had all that in Canada-whether through a king, a president or some other ruler?
I believe on the whole this is certainly not an extravagant amount for the coronation of our king, and the arrangement of the British commonwealth is the best which could be had, so far as Canada is concerned, when we consider it in terms of money. I believe the hon. member will be better advised not to raise all these questions just for the purpose- and he will forgive me for saying this-of criticizing. I 'have yet to see a proposal by this government which has been accepted by the hon. member. Surely some of our proposals must be deserving of approval and ought to he supported at times.
This afternoon the bon. member was very thin-skinned, and thought I was imputing motives to him. About five minutes before he had said that my right hon. leader was not sincere.
No, no.

I said that, as Hansard will show. It is strange that if the proposals of the government are considered to be in harmony with the will of the majority of the people, I should object to them in order to gain political prestige. It would be easy for some of us to float with the current

That is all very well, then. All I wish to say is that I am a little weary-
Oh, oh.

-of having people in this house shout at one simply because he states a position, on which he was elected, and on which he has been elected at election after election throughout the years.
The minister has a perfect right to introduce the estimates, but we, as part of the opposition, have a perfect right to criticize them. I do not intend to go over the ground again, but I do protest-and that is all I can do-against these very large expenditures which are not directly related even to the defence of the country, as must be admitted. This afternoon dire necessity was pleaded; someone suggested that war might come before July. If anything like that were true, surely we would expect those advocating military defence would spend every cent of the money in the defence of this country, instead of on a ceremonial affair in London. That is the basis of my criticism of the estimate. I again protest against this elaborate expenditure.

I wish to correct an erroneous impression left by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, when he referred1 to the soldiers being sent over. May I inform him that about eighty per cent of the amount spent is being spent on volunteer citizen soldiers in the militia forces of Canada. Many hon. members know those men, and every class he mentioned- the farmers, the labouring class, the business men, the fishermen, the miners-
But they go as soldiers, not as fishermen or miners.

No; they go in both capacities. They are citizens of Canada, and volunteer soldiers. To soldiering they give only a small amount of their time, as a patriotic duty. I feel certain that labourers, farmers, miners, officials and every single section of the community throughout Canada will be represented in the contingent to be sent. I think the hon. member either wittingly or otherwise conveyed an erroneous impression when he stated it was a military contingent. These men are volunteer soldiers who are rendering a magnificent service to Canada. As a matter of fact, some of them are actually on relief at the present time in some of the cities. They are performing a magnificent work in the militia service of Canada, So far as possible, every section of the community as well as every province should be represented in the coronation contingent.

I think it should be pointed out that up to date we have received only one interim report from this veterans' assistance commission. That report deals largely with the organization of the commission, and with the instructions that they sent out. It is really a very minor report. I believe that the delay in bringing down a more complete report from that commission is doing great harm because soldier organizations, right across Canada, expected great things of this veterans' assistance commission; the veterans themselves expected great things of the commission; and the special committee of this house which sat last year to deal with pensions and returned soldier problems also expected great things of this commission. All these bodies expected that the government would act on the report of this commission, and act during this session, not during the session of 1938. But now the position is this, that if these reports are not brought down very soon, it will be too late for the government to pass legislation this session, and there will be nothing done until 1938. That can be seen plainly by all interested parties, and I am afraid that the result will be grave dissatisfaction among veterans right across Canada.
Last year the soldier organizations who were represented before the pension committee, and the committee itself and the house all recognized that the principal soldier problem was the problem of the unemployed war veteran. This house passed the Veterans' Assistance Commission Act, which provided for setting up a veterans' assistance commission, and we also voted $500,000 with which they could do their work. The duties of this commission I think may be fairly summarized by saying they were to investigate the extent of unemployment among veterans, to classify the unemployed veterans, for example, as to whether they were employable or unemployable, and to ascertain their ages and occupations. The commission were also to try to find schemes for the employment of these unemployed veterans who are employable, and were supposed also to report on ways of caring for the unemployable veterans.
The organization of the commission took place in July of last year, and they have held public hearings across Canada, a great deal of interest being taken in the hearings in all centres, so that there are many thousands of people throughout the country waiting and watching for results from the commission. The commission have seen many industrialists and other employers of labour and have had questionnaires returned from 33,000 unemployed veterans. My suggestion is that by this time
the commission should have had figures available for consideration by this house, and yet, as I have said before, we have only one interim report outlining the organization of the commission and referring to two schemes which were recommended by one of the honorary local committees.
The Veterans' Assistance Commission Act provided for these honourary local committees, and according to this interim report they have been set up in ten cities. The report shows that 170 men have been appointed as members of these local committees, and these men are among the leading men in the different cities. I know that in Vancouver the minister has been able to get some of the best men in the city to act on the honorary local committee. These committees have held meetings and no doubt have made recommendations. They are really exploring a new field, trying to help get jobs for the unemployed veterans. They deserve great credit for that and should be given all possible assistance, but I have had this experience with the committee in Vancouver; they have asked me: " Suppose we do work out some scheme; how do we know that the government is not going to sidetrack it, like governments do? Are we not wasting our time in doing this work?" Now the last thing I want to see happen is for the government to give any justification for these committees to think that such is the case. If these local committees go out of business, if they lose interest, it will be fatal to the success of the Veterans' Assistance Commission Act and the whole plan will fail.
I suggest that the government should at once get from this veterans' assistance commission, and table in the house so that we can all study them, reports showing the extent of unemployment among the veterans, the classification of the unemployed, the schemes for employment that have been worked out by this commission, and what ways they have to suggest for caring for the veterans who are actually unemployable.
The minister said the other night that there were 33,000 unemployed veterans in Canada who had filled in and returned the questionnaire sent out by the commission. I think it would be a fair estimate that many thousands of these, perhaps 15,000, are unemployable. I suggest that the government should face this problem of the unemployable veterans right now; waiting will only make the problem worse. The commission can do nothing for them because they are unemployable ; no improvement in business conditions can help them because they are unemployable.

Are they simply to be kept on relief for another year? The government might as well decide now what they propose to do about this problem. If they do not, I am afraid that the unemployed veterans will lose confidence in the veterans' assistance commission and also in the government, because all their hopes are based upon action being taken by this commission and by the government during this year, not next year.
The special committee of this house which sat last year realized that early reports from the commission were absolutely necessary, and the minister will remember that we included in our report this recommendation:
To ensure that the progress of the commission's activities, both in connection with its surveys and application of approved projects, be made known to the government, your committee would also recommend that the commission be required to submit from time to time interim reports on matters arising out of the act.
In pursuance of that recommendation there was placed in the act at the beginning of section 12:
The minister may from time to time require the commission to submit a report on the progress of projects and other matters arising out of this act.
We were very keen that the commission should report as early as possible, because we realized that little could be done to deal with the problem of the unemployed soldier until we got a report from the commission. Some of us complained last year because there would have to be the delay of one year in getting action. This year we have come to Ottawa expecting to proceed on the basis of reports from this commission; all action was to be based on their suggestions. All the war veteran members of the house, regardless of party, are ready to help the government work out some reasonable solution for this problem. The question is above partisan politics. We are only too glad to help the minister and we realize that the problem is difficult, but in order to help him and to get on with this work we simply must have reports from this commission, and we must have them quickly; otherwise no help can be given to the unemployed veteran during the present session. I suggest to the minister that he put all possible pressure on the commission, that he get as many reports as possible and have them tabled as quickly as possible, so that we can do something during this session to help these men. He will find hon. members on this side only too glad to cooperate with him in facing the problem.

speechtext: In 1933-34 it was $26,000, of which $20,495.17 was spent; in 1934-35 it was $22,000, of which $20,183.76 was spent; in 1935-36 it was $21,000 and exactly $21,000 was spent; in 1936-37, prior to November 30, 1936, it was $20,000, and we have expended $14,270.73.
Pensions or salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: These are all pensions payable to militiamen who were on active service in the rebellion.

Item agreed to.
European war pensions, naval, militia, and air forces after the war, $41,500,000.

I -wish to pass one
comment on this item in connection with a case which apparently is outside the departmental regulations. A soldier named Thomas Cruden was gassed in the war. He is a Scotchman and was very diffident about making application, and finally he had to be sent to California by a fraternal organization to which he belonged. It seems that being in a hospital in California he cannot receive consideration from the department. I am not finding fault with the department, because I have found in the last year or two that a great number of cases I have been interested in have been taken care of, and I am convinced that there has been a great improvement in the way in which returned soldiers have been treated. I have no fault to find with what has been done in Canada; on the contrary I have a great deal of commendation and praise for the way in which the department is now looking after the returned men. This man, Thomas Cruden, is in a hospital in the United States, having been sent there by the fraternal organization to which he belongs, and because he is outside Canada it seems that he has no claim on the department. Is there any regulation under which he can come?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
If the gentleman has any claim for pension he can submit his claim from outside Canada as well as from within.

Mr. MaoNICOL: Will he be accorded his pension while in a hospital in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: He could get his pension wherever he happened to be unless we were paying for him, and then we would deduct a certain amount. He would probably get the pension awarded, him by the pension commission here. If he were in one of our own hospitals his pension would be taken away during the time he was in hospital if he went on pay and allowances, which would amount to much more in most cases.

He was ordered to California by his doctors and was sent there by this fraternal organization. I shall again report the case to the department and I feel confident that if anything can be done it will be done.

It was expected that the war veterans' commission would deal with those in receipt of small pensions, and I was endeavouring to point out to the minister that if we could gather some more accurate information as to his intentions with regard to the general problem, as far as he is able to divulge it, it would be of great assistance to us in the consideration of these estimates. With reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver South, I would remind the minister that it was recommended by a special committee last session that one of the first duties of the veterans' assistance commission would be to make a survey and submit suitable recommendations in regard to those veterans who at that time, it was urged, should receive the benefits of the War Veterans' Allowance Act. A formula was devised and those capable of maintaining themselves were put into one category. A classification was established for those between the ages of fifty-five and sixty, but it was not possible at that time to secure the approval of parliament for any lowering of the age limit. It was felt, however, that there was a large category that might not be covered by amendments to the act, and that their interests should be safeguarded by early recommendations from the veterans' assistance commission. Through the courtesy of the minister I have been given an opportunity of perusing this material and I approve everything done. But that does not bring us to the core of the problem and I submit that we have a right to expect from the veterans' assistance commission at an early date some interim report which would review the evidence given before the commission at its various sittings, give us some outline of the picture, the general distress existing among ex-service men, and 31111-75

recommend to the minister, and through him to parliament, some emergent remedial legislation.
I can sympathize with the minister in his statement that it is impossible to bring in a comprehensive plan with respect to a problem so complex and therefore I shall not harass him or press him. As stated by the hon. member for Vancouver South, however, the organized veterans, and the veterans generally throughout Canada patiently accepted the assurances given the house last session that after a proper inquiry was made and projects were formulated they would then receive the benefits they have a right to expect, particularly in the case of the unemployed. We are in danger of moving rapidly towards the close of the present session and the minister has not been able yet to suggest any adequate appropriation for men in this category. We would appreciate some assurance from him at an early date that such interim report may be had-not the material placed on the table this evening but an interim report which would to a degree at least meet the distress of which we find evidence on every hand, and, may I suggest, to relieve which he has more or less promised that some measures would be taken. I hope he will agree with the suggestion advanced by the hon. member for Vancouver South that the two votes be held over until we have an opportunity of reviewing the findings of the veterans' assistance commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My hon. friend has for the past week or more been so busily and vociferously and actively engaged in the arts of peace that I could reasonably expect he would soon be following his natural bent and engaging in the arts of war, but I am sorry that I should be the victim of his aggression without even having the right to declare my neutrality.
No defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
No defence whatsoever. But I may repeat what I said to the hon. member for Vancouver South, that an interim report was submitted to me some time ago. The matters contained therein are of such great importance that I thought it necessary to refer the report back to the committee for further details and clarification. When I have received a reply from the commission I shall be only too glad to table the report, and if at that time the government decide that action should be taken upon it I can assure my hon. friends that time will be found, or made, to permit of legislation being brought down. I cannot give any other assurance than that; I think that is fair enough in all conscience.

Can the minister tell
me how many veterans between fifty-five and sixty are receiving the burnt-out pension?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That again is war veterans' allowances. That comes under the legislation passed last session. Applications could come in only some time in July or August, and I think in the neighbourhood of six or seven hundred have been accepted so far. I shall be glad to furnish my hon. friend with full and specific details of that when we come to the appropriate item.

Would the minister kindly tell me what is the yearly contribution of General McNaughton to the pension fund since he has been seconded from the Department of National Defence to the Department of Trade and Commerce?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I have not the least idea, nor do I know how I could find that out, because no contributions are made to the Canadian pension commissioners. My hon. friend knows, I think, that the Militia Pension Act of 1901 is administered by the Canadian pension commissioners only to the extent that they pay out the amounts of money which are indicated to them by the Department of National Defence.
I thank the minister, and I ask him who will give me the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I suggest that the Department of National Defence could do it. I am sure I cannot.
Then I shall put a question on the order paper which will be answered by the Secretary of State.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
By the Department of
Finance in all probability.
Last year quite extensive amendments were made to the Pension Act. Would the minister tell the committee how they have worked out. I have had no complaints about them; they seem to be working well.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: If my hon. friend has 'had no complaints, doubtless they worked out well. I have before me a report from the chairman of the pension committee. It is lengthy; I do not think I need read it all.

Table it.
Mr. POW'ER: I could table it-no, it is more or less confidential. But I could give the high lights of it. The increased liability due to the addition of the widows who became entitled to pension-my hon. friend will remember that in certain circumstances widows not previously entitled to pension became eligible-amounted to $36,792. The reinstatement of additional allowances for housekeepers involved an increase of $24,388. The correction of marriage status involved an increase of $4,578; the increase due to pensions paid in respect of self-inflicted wounds was $5,388; perpetuation of errors in previous awards, $8,811. These actions in themselves show an increase in the annual liability of $79,957, which exceeds by $35,842 the total increase in annual liability. This latter figure may be taken as indicating what would have been the normal decrease had it not been for the enactment of the amendments of 1936. The fact that these sources of irritation and dissatisfaction have been removed at such moderate expense is a gratifying comment on the soundness of the action taken by the government.

When the minister next comes with his estimates before the committee, I should be greatly obliged if he could be in a position to indicate something as to 'the amount of the patriotic fund at the end of the South African war. Under the statutes passed last session the South African veterans who were burnt out are not eligible for any benefits. They used to receive benefits from the patriotic fund, but it will be recalled that that fund was exhausted in dealing with the soldiers of the great war. The number of South African veterans left is small. If the government contemplate legislation, I think something should be done in that regard. It will be recalled that we did not pay them; they were paid by the British government. Inasmuch as we assumed no financial responsibility with respect to them while in South Africa, and those who returned are now few in number-because I think the average would be between sixty and seventy-and are

in pretty bad shape, unable to work, not -receiving the benefits now -that they did get from the patriotic fund, and not eligible for pension under existing legislation, I trust the government will not overlook the claims of these unfortunate m-en, who are most deserving from the Standpoint of their present status.

When the committee was sitting last year, I made myself the advocate of the South African veterans, and I am only too happy to endorse what the leader of the opposition has said. Would a person who has served in the naval, military or air forces here in Canada but who did not go overseas be entitled to any of these Canadian pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: The air force was enlisted by the imperial government, so they would not be entitled to Canadian pensions. But any other man who enlisted in the Canadian forces was entitled to obtain a pension if he could prove that his disability was incurred in or was due to service.

Who did not go
overseas?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I must say the deadline for further applications for pension was set at July 1, 1936, for those who served only in Canada. So they are debarred by statute from making application now, although they had approximately twenty years to do so.

In connection with the amendment regarding the deadline, may I say that practically the only complaint I had last year in connection with pensions was that many of these men did not know that the deadline expired on July 1. What effort was made by the department to notify the different returned men's organizations that the deadline for soldiers who had not served overseas had been set?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The legislation was introduced about March 1, and was finally passed about the beginning of June, last year. In that period the question was debated and, as the hon. member knows, was discussed before a parliamentary committee. Returned soldiers' organizations were immediately made aware of the fact that there was to be a
deadline for certain cases in Canada. I was out at the Canadian Legion convention in Vancouver, and announced it there. I know that, generally speaking, the ex-soldiers' associations were quite familiar with the legislation proposed. I do not think there was much objection to it, from their standpoint. I shall have the figures available at a later time, but offhand I would say that about six cases have been turned down as being statute barred since then-not more than that.

I do not see how they
could be notified during the convention at Vancouver, because the amendment had not then been passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That it was the intention of the government to introduce such legislation.
That it was the intention?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.
What effort was made, after the amendment was passed? There were quite a number of complaints, and I believe the persons complaining thought they did not receive sufficient notice.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I think the deadline was set at July 1, 1936. The legislation was passed in June. I doubt whether it would have been possible, during that short period of time, to advise all ex-soldiers in Canada as to their rights under the legislation. But certainly all ex-solders' associations were fully aware of it.
I do not wish to prolong the debate, but the minister must bear in mind that all returned men do not belong to veterans' organizations.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I quite agree.
There were men who came to me and said they had absolutely no notice of the intention of the government to set a deadline at July 1.

I notice there is a reduction in the estimate of about $150,000 as compared with last year. I wonder whether this means that we have reached the peak in our pension expenditures, or whether it is just an estimate of the amount that has to be paid. Do I understand the cut-down on tine deadline was for soldiers who did not leave Canada?

I have in mind some men in my constituency who would be in this class: They served overseas, and I should like to have an answer to give them. They were gassed, and although they have no marks on them by way of wounds, as a result of the gas they have recently been unable to follow their occupations.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: There is no deadline for them, if they served overseas. That provision applies only to those who served in Canada.

I have received several letters from war veterans in western Canada, and especially from exprisoners of war, who complain that they are unable to obtain remuneration from the pensions department. They contend there are a great many pensioners employed at large salaries, and they feel that if there were a deadline whereby, after a man received say $2,000 per year, his pension would be discontinued, they would have a better opportunity of presenting their case and receiving a certain amount of money from the vote. Is it a fact that there is no limitation on the amount of salary a pensioner may receive?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Pension has nothing to do with the salary a man receives either from the government or from a private concern. It has always been held as a principle, from the very first pension committee, that the awarding of a pension to any ex-soldier should not debar him from any employment whatsoever. I do not know how the constituents of the hon. member in western Canada would be assisted in any way in establishing their claim for pensions if we were to take away from someone who already has a pension his (Mr. Power.]
right to earn a living or to earn a salary commensurate with his ability and1 capacity.
